title: Given a string containing the bracket characters round, square, and curly, determine whether every opening bracket is closed by the matching type in the correct order, using a stack.
shortTitle: Validate Balanced Parentheses Using a Stack

s1_definition.profdef: Balanced-parentheses validation uses a last-in-first-out stack to confirm that every opening bracket has a correctly typed and correctly ordered closing bracket. You push each opening bracket, and on each closing bracket you pop and check that the popped opener matches the closer's type. The string is valid only if every closer matched and the stack is empty at the end. It runs in linear time and linear worst-case space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India stacking approval slips on a spike. Every time a nested approval opens, she spikes a slip of that colour on top. When an approval closes, she can only remove the slip currently on top, and its colour must match the one closing. If a red approval tries to close while a blue slip sits on top, the paperwork is out of order and she rejects the batch. At the end the spike must be empty, meaning every approval that opened was properly closed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Push every opener, pop and type-match on every closer, and the string is valid only if the stack ends empty.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Balanced-parentheses validation uses a last-in-first-out stack to confirm that every opening bracket has a correctly typed and correctly ordered closing bracket. You push each opening bracket, and on each closing bracket you pop and check that the popped opener matches the closer's type. The string is valid only if every closer matched and the stack is empty at the end. It runs in linear time and linear worst-case space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India stacking approval slips on a spike. Every time a nested approval opens, she spikes a slip of that colour on top. When an approval closes, she can only remove the slip currently on top, and its colour must match the one closing. If a red approval tries to close while a blue slip sits on top, the paperwork is out of order and she rejects the batch. At the end the spike must be empty, meaning every approval that opened was properly closed.

**One line to remember:** Push every opener, pop and type-match on every closer, and the string is valid only if the stack ends empty.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is that brackets must close in the reverse order they opened, which is exactly the last-in-first-out behaviour a stack gives you. In Java the recommended stack is `ArrayDeque` used through the `Deque` interface rather than the legacy `Stack` class, because `Stack` extends `Vector` and is synchronised on every call, which is slower and rarely what you want. For example, `Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();` gives you `push`, `pop`, and `peek` without the synchronisation overhead.

As you scan the string left to right, for each opening bracket you call `stack.push(c)`, which places it on top. For each closing bracket you first check the stack is not empty, because a closer with nothing to match against is an immediate failure, then you `stack.pop()` the most recent opener and compare types. A clean way to compare is a small map from closer to its matching opener, for example `Map<Character,Character> pairs = Map.of(')','(', ']','[', '}','{');`, then the check is `if (stack.pop() != pairs.get(c)) return false;`.

Two end conditions matter. If at any closer the stack is empty, there is no opener to match, so you return false right away. After the full scan, the stack must be empty; if openers remain, they were never closed, so you return false. Only an empty stack at the end means true. Missing either check is the classic bug that passes a string like an unmatched opening bracket.

A senior-level nuance is the complexity and the variants. Time is linear because each character is pushed and popped at most once, and space is linear in the worst case of all openers. The same stack technique extends to validating nested expressions, matching HTML or XML tags, and checking balanced quotes in a parser, so interviewers use it as the gateway to stack-based parsing.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India ingests structured transaction messages whose nested segments are delimited by brackets, and a malformed message with mismatched brackets must be rejected before parsing, otherwise the downstream parser throws deep in processing and corrupts a batch. We need a fast pre-check that confirms the brackets are balanced. This is exactly what a stack-based validator does, because nesting must close in reverse order.

Problem 2 — A closing bracket that appears with no matching opener, or an opener left dangling at the end, both mean the message framing is broken. The stack naturally catches both: an empty stack on a closer is an early reject, and a non-empty stack at the end is a dangling-opener reject.

In our mini-project we build a `BracketValidator` with an `isBalanced` method over a message-framing string. The demo validates a correctly nested message and a broken one, logging each push and pop so you can watch the spike of slips grow and shrink.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the well-framed message of curly, square, round openers then matching closers, and the broken message where a round closer appears before the square it is nested in.

Step 1: For the good message, we read curly and push it, depth one. We read square and push it, depth two. We read round and push it, depth three.

Step 2: We read the round closer, pop the round opener, they match, depth two. We read the square closer, pop the square opener, they match, depth one. We read the curly closer, pop the curly opener, they match, depth zero.

Step 3: The scan ends with an empty stack, so the good message is balanced and we return true.

Step 4: For the bad message we push curly, square, round the same way, depth three. We then read the square closer while the round opener is on top. The popped opener is round, which does not match the square closer, so we immediately return false.

Step 5: Throughout, only the stack changed; the input string was read once left to right, confirming the linear time behaviour.

```
[2026-10-26 23:20:01] INFO    Message '{[()]}' balanced? true
[2026-10-26 23:20:01] WARNING   mismatch at ']' — invalid framing
[2026-10-26 23:20:01] INFO    Message '{[(])}' balanced? false
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Stack-Based Bracket Validation ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Stack (LIFO) via ArrayDeque — reverse-order matching         │
  │  Lookup map closer→opener for O(1) type check                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: BracketValidator only validates framing                   │
  │  O: new bracket types = add map entries, no logic change      │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           BracketValidator            │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - PAIRS: Map<Character,Character>    │
  │  + isBalanced(s: String): boolean     │  O(n) time, O(n) space
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Pre:  s contains only bracket chars
      Post: true iff every opener matched and stack empty

  ── State Diagram: Scan ──────────────────────────────────

  [reading] ──opener──→ push ──→ [reading]
  [reading] ──closer, match──→ pop ──→ [reading]
  [reading] ──closer, empty/mismatch──→ [INVALID]
  [end, stack empty] ──→ [VALID]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. isBalanced(s)
  2.   for each char: opener → push; closer → pop + match
  3.   empty-on-closer or type-mismatch → return false
  4.   return stack.isEmpty()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Validating balanced parentheses uses a last-in-first-out stack because brackets must close in the reverse order they opened. I scan the string once from left to right. For every opening bracket I push it onto the stack, and for every closing bracket I pop the most recent opener and confirm its type matches the closer. The string is valid only if every closer found a correctly typed match and the stack is completely empty at the end.

There are two failure conditions I always guard. If I hit a closing bracket while the stack is empty, there is no opener to match, so I return false immediately. And after the whole scan, if any openers remain on the stack, they were never closed, so that is also false. Only an empty stack at the end means the string is balanced. In Java I use ArrayDeque through the Deque interface rather than the old Stack class, because Stack extends Vector and synchronises every call, which is slower and unnecessary here.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this as a fast pre-check on structured transaction messages whose nested segments are delimited by brackets. A malformed message with crossed or dangling brackets gets rejected to a dead-letter path before it ever reaches the real parser, which protects a whole batch from a parser error deep in processing. The validator runs in linear time, scanning each character once, with worst-case linear space when everything is an opener.

The senior-level point I make is that this stack technique is the foundation of real parsing. The identical idea scales up to matching HTML and XML tags, validating nested expressions, and checking balanced quotes, and it is the first step toward shunting-yard expression evaluation. So I treat it not as a toy puzzle but as the simplest instance of stack-based syntactic validation that appears throughout production parsers.
